Hash-map collision handling is a fundamental concept in computer science, essential for maintaining the efficiency of hash tables, which are data structures that map keys to values for fast retrieval. A hash map uses a hash function to convert a key into an array index. However, because the range of possible keys is often much larger than the size of the underlying array, different keys can produce the same hash value, a scenario known as a collision. If not handled correctly, collisions can degrade performance from O(1) average time complexity to O(n) in the worst case. There are two primary methods for handling these collisions: chaining and open addressing.

Chaining, also known as separate chaining, is one of the most intuitive collision resolution strategies. In this approach, each array index, or "bucket," contains a linked list (or another dynamic data structure like a balanced tree) of entries that hash to that index. When a collision occurs, the new entry is simply appended to the list at that bucket. For example, consider a hash table of size 5. If the hash function maps both "apple" and "banana" to index 2, the table at index 2 will hold a list containing both entries. When searching for "apple," the system hashes "apple"

Hash-map collision handling is a fundamental concept in computer science, essential for maintaining the efficiency of hash tables, which are data structures that map keys to values for fast retrieval. A hash map uses a hash function to convert a key into an array index. However, because the range of possible keys is often much larger than the size of the underlying array, different keys can produce the same hash value, a scenario known as a collision. If not handled correctly, collisions can degrade performance from O(1) average time complexity to O(n) in the worst case. There are two primary methods for handling these collisions: chaining and open addressing.

Chaining, also known as separate chaining, is one of the most intuitive collision resolution strategies. In this approach, each array index, or "bucket," contains a linked list (or another dynamic data structure like a balanced tree) of entries that hash to that index. When a collision occurs, the new entry is simply appended to the list at that bucket. For example, consider a hash table of size 5. If the hash function maps both "apple" and "banana" to index 2, the table at index 2 will hold a list containing both entries. When searching for "apple," the system hashes "apple"
